content: 1. Mass drug administration involves the distribution of anthelmintic medications to entire populations within a defined geographical area (e.g., state, region, province, district, sub-district, village) at regular intervals, regardless of the infection status of individuals. 2. Targeted chemotherapy focuses on specific groups, such as school-age children, who are given anthelmintic medications at regular intervals, irrespective of their individual infection status. 3. Selective chemotherapy is implemented after a systematic screening of a population living in areas endemic to soil-transmitted helminths. Individuals identified or suspected to be infected are treated with anthelmintic medications. 4. School-age children are defined as those between the ages of 5 and 12 years. Although many children in this age group may not attend school, these years are typically considered compulsory school years in most settings, providing an opportunity to address their nutritional needs. In some contexts, the upper age limit may extend to 14 years. 5. Soil-transmitted helminthiases refer to parasitic diseases caused by soil-transmitted helminths. The four main species of nematodes responsible for these infections are the roundworm (Ascaris lumbricoides), the whipworm (Trichuris trichiura), and the hookworms (Necator americanus and Ancylostoma duodenale). 6. Women of reproductive age include post-menarcheal adolescent girls and adult women, including those who are pregnant or lactating, typically between the ages of 15 and 49. This age range may vary depending on the context. 7. Globally, in 2010, soil-transmitted helminth infections accounted for 18 million disability-adjusted life years. Approximately 820 million people were infected with roundworms, 460 million with whipworms, and 440 million with hookworms. Despite species-specific characteristics, these infections are grouped together for control purposes due to their similar geographic endemicity, affected at-risk groups, treatment with the same medications, diagnostic tools, and mechanisms of health impact linked to infection intensity. 8. The purpose of the guideline is to provide global, evidence-based recommendations on preventive chemotherapy as a public health intervention in areas endemic for soil-transmitted helminths. The goal is to reduce the worm burden in children, adolescent girls, women of reproductive age, and pregnant women, including those co-infected with HIV. 9. The recommendations are intended for policymakers, technical experts, and program staff involved in designing, implementing, and expanding programs to control soil-transmitted helminth infections and improve public health through nutrition-sensitive actions and safe, hygienic environments. 10. Preventive chemotherapy (deworming) using annual or biannual single-dose albendazole (400 mg) or mebendazole (500 mg) is recommended for all young children (12–23 months), preschool children (24–59 months), and school-age children living in areas where the baseline prevalence of soil-transmitted helminth infections is 20% or higher among children. This intervention aims to reduce the worm burden (strong recommendation, low-quality evidence). Biannual administration is recommended where the baseline prevalence exceeds 50%. 11. Preventive chemotherapy is also recommended for non-pregnant adolescent girls (10–19 years) and non-pregnant women of reproductive age (15–49 years) in areas where the baseline prevalence of soil-transmitted helminth infections is 20% or higher among these groups. This intervention aims to reduce the worm burden (strong recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). Biannual administration is recommended where the baseline prevalence exceeds 50%. 12. For pregnant women, preventive chemotherapy using single-dose albendazole (400 mg) or mebendazole (500 mg) is recommended after the first trimester in areas where the baseline prevalence of hookworm and/or Trichuris trichiura infections is 20% or higher among pregnant women, and anemia is a severe public health problem (prevalence of 40% or higher among pregnant women). This intervention aims to reduce the worm burden of hookworm and Trichuris trichiura infections (conditional recommendation, moderate-quality evidence). 13. Preventive chemotherapy, or the periodic large-scale administration of anthelmintic medications to at-risk populations, can significantly reduce the burden of soil-transmitted helminth infections. However, it does not interrupt the cycle of infection and reinfection. Populations living in contaminated environments remain at risk and require frequent administration of anthelmintic medications. 14. Multisectoral, integrated programs are necessary to maximize and sustain the benefits of reduced worm burden. These programs should address the underlying environmental and social determinants of soil-transmitted helminth infections. 15. The guideline development process included identifying priority questions, retrieving and synthesizing evidence, formulating recommendations, and planning for dissemination, implementation, and impact evaluation. The GRADE methodology was used to assess the quality of evidence and guide the formulation of recommendations. 16. Available evidence included systematic reviews of randomized controlled trials assessing the effects of preventive chemotherapy on controlling soil-transmitted helminth infections in various at-risk groups. Studies compared participants receiving anthelmintic medications with those receiving a placebo or no treatment. 17. Preventive chemotherapy is well-tolerated, with only minor and transient side effects reported. It is widely accepted among beneficiaries and implementers, and the logistical challenges and costs of alternative methods to identify and treat infected individuals are prohibitive. 18. The current guideline updates and supersedes previous recommendations and complements operational guidance for helminth control in school-age children.
